title: Painting a timber garden fence with fence paint
subtitle: Apply a water-based or spirit-based fence paint to protect and colour softwood fence panels and posts
excerpt: How to prepare and paint a timber garden fence with fence treatment or fence paint. Covers cleaning, preparing the timber, applying paint with a brush and roller, and the second coat.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK decorating trade practice.

glossaryTerms.definition: A water- or spirit-based coating formulated for exterior softwood. Fence paint contains preservative, UV stabilisers, and mould inhibitors. It is thicker and more pigmented than a wood stain, providing an opaque finish. Most brands cover in two coats applied in the same session.

content.text: protects softwood fence panels from rot and UV damage and refreshes the garden boundary. The prep work takes longer than the painting: clean wood takes paint well; dirty or wet wood rejects it. Work on a dry day with no rain forecast for 24 hours.

Brush off loose dirt, moss, and lichen with a stiff-bristled brush. For green algae growth, apply a dilute fungicidal wash (available from garden centres and DIY stores) and allow it to kill the growth before brushing off. Allow the fence to dry for at least a day after washing, ideally longer. Sand any rough splinters with a sanding block. Remove any loose or flaking old paint with the sanding block or a scraper. You do not need to strip the fence down to bare wood; clean, sound old paint provides a good base.

Fold a dust sheet or polythene along the fence base to protect the plants and paving immediately in front of the fence. Fence paint splashes land on foliage and paving and are very difficult to remove. Move potted plants away from the fence line before you start.

Stir the fence paint thoroughly before use. Use the 9-inch roller for the open faces of the fence panels and the 50 mm brush to work paint into the gaps between the panel slats and around the posts. Work from the top of the fence panel down. The roller gives fast coverage on the flat faces; the brush picks up the ends of the slats and the detail around the rails. Apply the first coat fairly liberally to allow the paint to soak into the timber.

Allow the first coat to dry for the time stated on the tin (typically two to four hours for water-based fence paints at normal temperature). Apply the second coat in the same way. The second coat will be lighter to apply as the first coat has closed the grain. Two coats give the correct film build for the stated durability period (often five to seven years).

Rinse water-based fence paint from the roller and brushes immediately with cold water. Spirit-based fence paint requires white spirit for cleaning tools. Fence paint in the roller tray will skin over if left even for a short break; cover the tray with a damp cloth or cling film while you break.

attrs.cause: The fence was not dry enough when painted, or old flaky paint was not removed first.
attrs.fix: Strip the peeling paint with a sanding block, allow the fence to dry, and repaint. Peeling is almost always a prep failure, not a paint failure.

attrs.symptom: Brush marks visible on the panel faces
attrs.cause: Paint applied too dry or with an overloaded brush on a hot day.
attrs.fix: Use the roller for flat panel faces; the roller leaves a fine stipple texture rather than brush lines. On very hot days, paint early in the morning before the surface heats up.
